p: The date of the work is uncertain. Gunadhya may have flourished under a Satavahana king of Pratishthana, the modern Paithan in Maharashtra; according to D. C. Sircar he probably lived between the 1st century BCE and the 3rd century CE. Another account, in the Nepala Mahatmya of the Skanda Purana, makes him a native of Mathura and court poet of King Madana of Ujjain, a tradition Sircar calls less authentic. Paishachi, the language he used, is a little-known Prakrit, described as the speech of the common people of the border regions of northwest India.

The earliest surviving reference seems to be that of Subandhu in his Vasavadatta, and Banabhatta refers to the work in the Harshacharita and the Kadambari. Dandin, in the Kavyadarsha, calls it marvellous and says it was composed in the vernacular of the bhutas, though his information appears to be second-hand. A Cambodian inscription of about 875 names Gunadhya, and the Kannada Kavirajamarga of about 850 mentions a Sanskrit version, now lost, by Durvinita. A romantic work by Gunadhya can safely be assumed to have existed before 600 CE.

The adaptations differ too much for the original to be reconstructed whole, but what they share allows strong inferences. The life of Udayana of Kaushambi served as a prelude: his upbringing in a hermitage after a monstrous bird carried off his pregnant mother, his captivity under Pradyota, king of Ujjayini, his elopement with Pradyota's daughter Vasavadatta, and his second marriage to Padmavati, arranged by ministers who made him believe Vasavadatta dead. The central story was that of their son Naravahanadatta, born as a boon of Kubera and fated to become emperor of the Vidyadharas. Kshemendra's version is in eighteen books called lambakas, as the original is thought to have been.

Besides the two Kashmiri versions, the story is known from the Sanskrit Brihatkathashlokasamgraha of Budhasvamin, of which the complete text has not been found, and from the Perunkatai and the Vasudevahimdi in vernacular languages. Dandin states that the original was in prose, not in the verse of the Kashmiri recensions. Scholars compare Gunadhya with Vyasa and Valmiki, and the disappearance of his text is counted a very great loss to Indian literature.

notes: Diacritics dropped to match the site's spelling (Paiśācī -> Paishachi, Bṛhatkathāślokasaṃgraha -> Brihatkathashlokasamgraha, Kauśāmbī -> Kaushambi, etc.).
The article dates Subandhu '600-700 CE' yet says the work is attested 'in the 6th century CE' by Dandin, Subandhu and Bana; I gave no date for Subandhu and used the article's 'before 600 CE'.

Left out: the Vikramaditya paragraph and 'Gunadhya may have lived around 78 CE' (from identifying King Satavahana with Shalivahana), which are weakly put in the article; the legendary divine origin, which the article only refers to a diagram for.
The article lists the Perunkatai and Vasudevahimdi only as 'in vernaculars' (not named as Tamil/Prakrit), so I did not name the languages.
